source_text: Verum quoniam de tantis et talibus rebus disserentibus non suffieit humanis sensibus et communi intellectui summam rei committere et, ut ita dixerim, visibiliter de invisibilibus pronuntiare, assumenda sunt nobis ad probationem horum, quae dicimus, etiam divinarum scripturarum testimonia. Quae testimonia ut certam et indubitatam "tree d o habeant fidem sive in his, quae dicenda a nobis, sive quae iam dicta sunt, necessarium prius videtur ostendere quod ipsae scripturae divinae sint, id est dei spiritu inspiratae. lgitur quam poterimus breviter etiam de hoc adsignabimus ex ipsis divinis scripturis quae nos conpetenter moverint proferentes, id est de Moyseo primo, legislatore gentis Hebraeae, et ex verbis lesu Christi, auctoris et principis Christianorum religionis et dogmatis. Cum enim permulti legislatores extiterint apud Graecos et barbaros, innumeri quoque doctores vel philosophi veritatem se pollicentes adserere, nullum meminimus legislatorem adfectum quendam et studium etiam exterarum gentium animis inicere potuisse, ut leges suas vel susciperent libenter vel cum omni animi intentione defenderent. Nemo ergo eam quae sibi visa est veritatem non solum pluribus aliis exteris nationibus, ‚sed ne uni quidem genti ita insinuare atque inolescere potuit, ut ad omnes eius scientia vel credulitas perveniret. Et quidem dubitari non potest quod et legislatores optaverint observari ab omnibus, si fieri posset, hominibus leges suas, et magistri, omnibus innotescere eam quae sibi visa fuerat veritatem. Sed scientes quia id omnino non possent, nee virtus in eis aliqua tanta subsisteret, quae etiam exteras nationes ad legum suarum vel adsertionum observantiam provocaret, ne conari quidem hoc aut incipere omnino ausi sunt, ne inprudentes eos etiam in hoc inefficax et inexplebile notaret inceptum. At vero in omni orbe terrarum, in omni Graecia atque universis exteris nationibus innumeri sunt et inmensi, qui relictis patris legibus et his, quos putabant deos, ad observantiam Moysi legis et discipulatum se Christi ceultumque tradiderunt, et hoc non sine ingenti odio adversum se commoto eorum, qui simulacra venerantur, ita ut ab his frequenter et cruciatibus adfligantur, nonnumquam etiam agantur in mortem; amplectuntur tamen et cum omni affectu custodiunt doctrinae Christi sermonem. Et est videre quomodo brevi tempore ipsa religio creverit, poenis eultorum mortibusque proficiens, sed et bonorum direptionibus atque omni ab his suppliciorum genere tolerato; et eo maxime mirum est quod ne doctores quidem ipsi vel satis idonei sunt vel satis plures: “praedicatur’ tamen sermo iste -in omni orbe terrarum”, ita ut ‘Graeci ac barbari, sapientes et insipientes’ religionem Christianae doctrinae suscipiant. Ex quo dubium non est “non haec humanis’ viribus aut ‘opibus” agi, ut cum omni potestate et creduhtate sermo Christi lesu apud omnium mentes atque animos convalescat. Nam et praedicta esse ab eo haec ipsa et divinis ab eo responsis confirmata, manifestum est cum dicit quia “apud praesides et iudices adducemini propter me, in testimonium ipsis et gentibuse; et rursum: “Praedieabitur hoe evangelium in omnibus gentibus”; et iterum: “Multi mihi dicent in illa die: Domine, domine, nonne in tuo nomine mandueavimus et bibimus, et in tuo nomine daemonia eiecimus? et dicam eis: Discedite a me, operarii iniquitatis s numquam cognovi vosc”. Quae si ita quidem dicta ab eo fuissent nee tamen ad finem ea, quae praedicta sunt, pervenissent, fortassis minus esse vera viderentur nec habere aliquid auctoritatis. Nune vero cum in effectum res, quae fuerant ab eo praedictae, perveniant, cum tanta autem potestate atque auctoritate praedictae sint, manifestissime declaratur deum vere esse, qui homo factus salutaria praecepta hominibus tradidit.
pass_a_gloss: But since it is not enough for human senses and common understanding to commit the sum of the matter and, so to speak, visibly pronounce on invisible things, we must also take up the testimonies of divine scriptures for proof of what we say. Which testimonies, so that they may have certain and undoubted faith, either in the things that must be said by us or in the things that have already been said, it seems necessary to show first that the scriptures themselves are divine, that is, inspired by the Spirit of God. Therefore, we will briefly assign also this from the divine scriptures themselves, which have moved us competently, producing from Moses, the first lawgiver of the Hebrew nation, and from the words of Jesus Christ, the author and principle of the Christian religion and doctrine. For when many lawgivers have existed among the Greeks and barbarians, and innumerable doctors or philosophers have promised to assert the truth, we do not remember any lawgiver who could have instilled a certain affection and study even in the minds of foreign nations, so that they would either willingly receive his laws or defend them with all intention of their mind. No one, therefore, could have insinuated and made the truth that seemed to him not only to many other foreign nations but also to one nation alone, so that his knowledge or credulity would reach all. And indeed, it cannot be doubted that lawgivers have wished their laws to be observed by all men, if it could be done, and masters that the truth that seemed to them would become known to all. But knowing that they could not do this at all, nor did such great virtue subsist in them that it would even provoke foreign nations to observe their laws or assertions, they did not even dare to try or begin this, lest they be noted as imprudent and ineffectual in this undertaking. But in the whole world, in all of Greece, and in all foreign nations, there are innumerable and immense people who, having abandoned the laws of their fathers and the gods they thought were gods, have given themselves to the observance of Moses' law and the discipleship of Christ, and this not without great hatred having been stirred up against them by those who venerate idols, so that they are frequently afflicted with torments and sometimes even led to death; yet they embrace and guard the doctrine of Christ's word with all affection. And it is evident how the religion itself has grown in a short time, profiting from the punishments and deaths of its cultivators, and also from the plundering of goods and every kind of suffering tolerated by them; and it is especially wonderful that not even the doctors themselves are sufficient or numerous enough: 'the word is preached' nonetheless 'in the whole world', so that 'Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish' receive the religion of Christian doctrine. From which it is not doubtful that 'these things are not done by human strength or resources', so that the word of Christ Jesus may grow strong with all power and credibility in the minds and souls of all. For it is manifest that these things were predicted by him and confirmed by divine responses, when he says that 'you will be led before rulers and judges on account of me, as a testimony to them and to the nations'; and again: 'This gospel will be preached in all nations'; and again: 'Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, did we not eat and drink in your name, and cast out demons in your name? And I will say to them: Depart from me, workers of iniquity, for I never knew you'. Which things, if they had been said by him and yet had not come to pass, would perhaps seem less true and would not have any authority. But now, since the things that were predicted by him have come to pass, and have been predicted with such great power and authority, it is most clearly declared that God truly exists, who, having become man, handed down salutary precepts to men.

pass_b_english: When people discuss matters so great and of such a kind, human senses and common understanding are not enough to entrust the heart of the matter to them, nor, so to speak, to pronounce visibly on invisible things. Therefore we must also bring forward the testimonies of divine scriptures to prove what we say. So that these testimonies may carry certain and undoubted conviction—whether for what we still must say or for what has already been said—it seems necessary to show first that the scriptures themselves are divine, that is, inspired by the Spirit of God. We will therefore set this out briefly from the divine scriptures themselves, the ones that have competently moved us to speak: from Moses, the first lawgiver of the Hebrew nation, and from the words of Jesus Christ, the author and principle of the Christian religion and doctrine.

Many lawgivers arose among the Greeks and barbarians, and innumerable teachers or philosophers promised to proclaim the truth. Yet we recall no lawgiver who could instill any affection or zeal even in the minds of foreign nations, so that they would either accept his laws willingly or defend them with their whole heart. Consequently, no one managed to insinuate and settle the truth that seemed right to him into so much as a single foreign nation, let alone many, so that his knowledge or credulity would reach everyone. Indeed, it cannot be doubted that lawgivers wished their laws to be observed by all people, if that were possible, and that teachers wanted the truth as they saw it to become known to all. But knowing they could not do this at all, and that no virtue of theirs was great enough even to provoke foreign nations to observe their laws or assertions, they did not even dare to try or begin, lest they be marked as imprudent and ineffectual in the undertaking.

Yet throughout the whole world, in all Greece, and in all foreign nations, there are innumerable and immense multitudes who have abandoned the laws of their fathers and the beings they thought were gods, and have given themselves over to the observance of Moses' law and the discipleship of Christ. They have done this despite the great hatred stirred up against them by those who venerate idols, so that they are frequently afflicted with torments and sometimes even led to death. Still they embrace and guard the doctrine of Christ's word with all affection. It is evident how the religion itself has grown in a short time, advancing through the punishments and deaths of its adherents, and also through the plundering of their goods and every kind of suffering they endured. It is especially remarkable that not even the teachers themselves are sufficiently qualified or numerous; yet 'the word is preached' (Matt 24:14) 'in the whole world', so that 'Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish' receive the religion of Christian doctrine.

From this there is no doubt that 'these things are not done by human strength or resources', so that the word of Christ Jesus may grow strong with all power and credibility in the minds and souls of all. For it is manifest that these very things were predicted by him and confirmed by divine responses. He said, 'you will be led before rulers and judges on account of me, as a testimony to them and to the nations' (Matt 10:18); and again, 'This gospel will be preached in all nations' (Matt 24:14); and again, 'Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, did we not eat and drink in your name, and cast out demons in your name? And I will say to them: Depart from me, workers of iniquity, for I never knew you' (Matt 7:22-23). If these things had been said by him yet had not come to pass, they would perhaps seem less true and carry no authority. But now, since the things he predicted have come to pass, and were predicted with such great power and authority, it is most clearly declared that God truly exists—the One who, having become man, handed down salutary precepts to men.
